To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) The economic burden associated with the selected rare diseases appears to vary significantly, ranging from a low to a moderate burden for most of them, and a high to very high burden for a minority of them (CF, Haemophilia); (2) Direct costs are generally found to be higher for the selected rare conditions than the average costs associated with common diseases; (3) Indirect costs are generally found, when available, to be higher than direct costs for the selected rare diseases,
(1) Cost of illness evidence on rare diseases is very limited, with only a small number of studies available for most diseases.

(a) there is a lack of cost of illness data for the majority of rare diseases, and (b) the evidence available shows that the majority of rare conditions are associated with significant direct and indirect economic burden, which can vary considerably between diseases.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and validation of a new instrument for measuring the economic burden of rare diseases.
the economic burden associated with rare diseases in Europe.
the development of a methodology for the economic evaluation of rare diseases, and with the development of an evidence-based cost of illness database for a number of rare diseases.
